subject: chemistry

items.q: What is meant by corrosion?
items.correct: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with the environment
items.misconception: Damage suffered only by metals, caused by oxygen in the air
items.why: Every classroom example is a metal, so the general definition gets quietly narrowed to metals. The specification defines corrosion as the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Stone buildings attacked by acidic gases are corroding too.
items.random_wrong: The rusting of iron that has been left outside in the wet

items.q: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?
items.correct: Both air and water in contact with the iron surface
items.misconception: Water alone; the air around the iron plays no part in it
items.why: Every rusty object a student has seen was wet at some point, while air is invisible and always there, so it never registers as a variable that could be removed. A nail in water that has been boiled to drive off dissolved air and sealed under oil does not rust, even though it is soaking wet. The only thing missing is air, so air must be necessary too.
items.random_wrong: Air alone, since rust is simply an oxide of iron

items.q: A nail is put in a tube of water that has been boiled and then covered with a layer of oil. After a week the nail has not rusted. What does this show?
items.correct: Water on its own cannot rust iron, so air is needed
items.misconception: The layer of oil is what stopped the nail rusting here
items.why: Oil is a barrier method in the very same topic, so it is read as the variable rather than as the seal that removes air. The oil never touches the nail; it floats on the water. Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil layer stops more dissolving back, so the only difference from the control is the absence of air.
items.random_wrong: Rusting needs only air, so the water was never needed

items.q: A nail is sealed in a tube of air with anhydrous calcium chloride at the bottom. After a week it has not rusted. What does this show?
items.correct: Dry air cannot rust iron, so water is needed
items.misconception: Calcium chloride is a chemical that prevents rust
items.why: Students expect any added chemical to act on the nail directly, rather than to change the air around it. The calcium chloride sits at the bottom of the tube, not on the nail. It is a drying agent: it removes water so that air can be tested on its own.
items.random_wrong: Air plays no part in the rusting of iron at all

items.q: Which method prevents corrosion by acting as a barrier?
items.correct: Painting the surface so that air and water cannot reach the metal
items.misconception: Bolting blocks of magnesium along the outside of the pipe
items.why: Zinc is applied as a coating, so it is filed with the barrier methods and its reactivity is never considered. The specification calls these coatings reactive. Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so even at a scratch the zinc reacts first and the iron is left alone.
items.random_wrong: Heating the metal strongly to harden its outside layer

items.q: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?
items.correct: An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
items.misconception: Aluminium is unreactive, so nothing in the air can attack it
items.why: Aluminium objects look clean and shiny for years, and 'does not corrode' is read as 'does not react', which contradicts its place in the reactivity series. Aluminium is more reactive than iron. It reacts fast with oxygen, but the oxide it makes sticks to the surface as a tough layer that stops anything reaching the metal below.
items.random_wrong: Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh clean metal behind

items.q: Iron sheets are galvanised. What does this mean?
items.correct: They are coated with zinc, which is more reactive
items.misconception: They are coated with tin, a metal that resists corrosion
items.why: 'Resists corrosion' sounds like the property you want, so the less reactive metal seems the safer choice. Sacrificial protection needs a metal MORE reactive than the one being protected, so that it corrodes first. A scratched tin can rusts faster than bare iron, because iron is now the more reactive metal in contact with tin.
items.random_wrong: They are dipped in acid to clean them before painting

items.q: A galvanised bucket is scratched right through to the iron. Why does the iron still not rust?
items.correct: The zinc corrodes away in place of the iron
items.misconception: The zinc melts and seals the scratch up again
items.why: Zinc is applied as a coating, so it is filed with the barrier methods and its reactivity is never considered. The specification calls these coatings reactive. Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so even at a scratch the zinc reacts first and the iron is left alone.
items.random_wrong: The iron corrodes first and so protects the zinc

items.q: Blocks of metal are bolted to a steel ship's hull to give sacrificial protection. Which metal should be used?
items.correct: Magnesium, as it is more reactive than iron and corrodes first
items.misconception: Copper, because it is less reactive and resists corrosion
items.why: 'Resists corrosion' sounds like the property you want, so the less reactive metal seems the safer choice. Sacrificial protection needs a metal MORE reactive than the one being protected, so that it corrodes first. A scratched tin can rusts faster than bare iron, because iron is now the more reactive metal in contact with tin.
items.random_wrong: Tin, because it sits below iron and will not be eaten away

items.q: Why are most metals in everyday use alloys rather than pure metals?
items.correct: The mixture has properties, like hardness, that suit the job
items.misconception: Alloys are compounds, so they cannot react with air at all
items.why: 'Made from two metals' sounds like a chemical combination, and the everyday word 'mixture' feels too weak for something as solid as brass. There is no reaction and no fixed formula. The proportions can be varied, and the atoms are simply mixed, which is why different sized atoms distort the layers and make the alloy harder.
items.random_wrong: Mixing metals always makes them much softer and easier to bend

items.q: Which statement about bronze is correct?
items.correct: It is an alloy of copper mixed with tin
items.misconception: It is copper mixed with zinc in fixed amounts
items.why: Both alloys are copper based and both names are old and unhelpful, so the second metal is easy to swap over. Fix it by the pairing the specification gives: bronze - tin, brass - zinc. Brass instruments and door fittings are brass; statues and bells are bronze.
items.random_wrong: It is a compound formed from copper and tin

items.q: Brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings. What is brass?
items.correct: A mixture of copper and zinc
items.misconception: A mixture of copper and pure tin
items.why: Both alloys are copper based and both names are old and unhelpful, so the second metal is easy to swap over. Fix it by the pairing the specification gives: bronze - tin, brass - zinc. Brass instruments and door fittings are brass; statues and bells are bronze.
items.random_wrong: A compound of copper and zinc

items.q: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy. Which metals is the gold usually mixed with?
items.correct: The gold is mixed with silver, copper and zinc
items.misconception: Nothing else, since jewellery gold is pure
items.why: Advertising treats 'pure gold' as the mark of quality, and carat numbers are read as a brand rather than a proportion. Pure gold is too soft for a ring worn every day. Silver, copper and zinc harden it, and the carat number states how much gold is present: 24 carat is 100%, 18 carat is 75%.
items.random_wrong: Iron and carbon, added to harden the gold

items.q: A ring is stamped 18 carat. What does this tell you about the ring?
items.correct: It is 75% gold, because 24 carat means pure gold
items.misconception: It contains 18% gold and 82% of other metals
items.why: Percentages are the familiar scale, so an unfamiliar number is assumed to be one, and the fixed total of 24 is never noticed. The scale runs to 24, not to 100. Divide by 24: 24/24 is 100% and 18/24 is 75%. So 18 carat gold is three quarters gold.
items.random_wrong: It is pure gold and it weighs 18 carats on a balance

items.q: How does high carbon steel differ from low carbon steel?
items.correct: High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer
items.misconception: High carbon steel is soft and easy to shape; low carbon steel is brittle
items.why: Carbon is met as graphite in pencils, which is soft and slippery, and that image is transferred to steel. The carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and jam the layers so they cannot slide. That makes the steel hard and strong, but also brittle, so it snaps rather than bends.
items.random_wrong: High carbon steel resists corrosion; low carbon steel rusts very fast

items.q: Why is stainless steel chosen for cutlery and sinks?
items.correct: It is hard and it resists corrosion well
items.misconception: It is pure iron, so there is nothing to rust
items.why: 'Stainless' sounds like clean and pure, and carbon is the only steel additive most students can name. Stainless steel is an alloy, not a pure metal, and the additions that matter are chromium and nickel. Carbon controls hardness and brittleness, not corrosion resistance.
items.random_wrong: It has extra carbon in it, which stops any rust

items.q: Aluminium alloys are used for the bodies of aircraft. Which property makes them suitable?
items.correct: They are low density, so a given volume of them weighs less
items.misconception: They are the strongest metals known, so they never bend
items.why: Aircraft are impressive and strong, so every property of the material used is assumed to be superior. Density and strength are different quantities. The reason aluminium alloys suit aircraft is that a given volume of them weighs less, so the plane is lighter to lift.
items.random_wrong: They are dense, so they are tough enough for an aircraft.

items.q: Duralumin is an alloy of aluminium with copper and magnesium. Its density is 2.8 g/cm3 and it is harder than pure aluminium. A titanium alloy has a density of 4.5 g/cm3 and is harder than duralumin. Which is the better choice for a lightweight bicycle frame that must not bend?
items.correct: Duralumin, because it is far less dense and still hard
items.misconception: Titanium alloy, because it is the harder of the two
items.why: One property is easier to compare than several, so the comparison stops at the first number in the table. An aircraft body made of the strongest steel would be too heavy to fly. Selecting a material means matching all the properties to the use, which is why data tables give several columns.
items.random_wrong: Titanium alloy, because a denser metal is always stronger

items.q: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?
items.correct: Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
items.misconception: Sand on its own, melted in a hot furnace
items.why: Demonstrations always stress that glass comes from sand, and the other two ingredients are less memorable. Sand alone melts only at a very high temperature. The specification gives three ingredients for soda-lime glass: sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
items.random_wrong: Sand with boron trioxide, heated strongly

items.q: How does borosilicate glass differ from soda-lime glass?
items.correct: It melts at a higher temperature
items.misconception: It melts at a much lower temperature
items.why: 'Used in a Bunsen flame' gets muddled into 'melts easily', when the reason it is used there is the opposite. Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures. That is exactly why it survives being heated when ordinary glass would not.
items.random_wrong: It is made from pure sand and nothing else

items.q: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?
items.correct: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace
items.misconception: Clay is melted and poured into a cold mould
items.why: Every other shaping process the student has met - casting metals, moulding glass - starts by melting, so the same route is assumed for clay. Clay is shaped while it is wet and soft. Heating in a furnace afterwards is what hardens it permanently; it is never melted.
items.random_wrong: Dry clay powder is pressed and left to set

items.q: LD and HD poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. Why do they have different properties?
items.correct: A different catalyst and conditions are used
items.misconception: They are built from two different monomers
items.why: Different product implies different starting material, which is usually a safe rule and fails here. The specification says the properties of a polymer depend on the monomer AND on the conditions of manufacture. Same ethene, different catalyst and conditions, two different materials.
items.random_wrong: HD poly(ethene) is pressed hard after it is made

items.q: Why do thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated?
items.correct: Separate chains are held only by weak forces
items.misconception: The strong covalent bonds along the chains break
items.why: Melting is assumed to mean bond breaking, and the only bonds the student has labelled in the chain are the covalent ones. Melting separates chains from one another; it does not break the chains themselves. Only the weak forces between the tangled chains have to be overcome.
items.random_wrong: Any solid will melt if it is heated enough

items.q: Why do thermosetting polymers keep their shape when they are heated?
items.correct: Cross-links join the chains to each other
items.misconception: They only melt above about a thousand degrees
items.why: 'Everything melts eventually' is a reasonable rule for simple molecular and metallic solids, and it is carried over without checking the structure. The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart. Heating strongly chars or burns the polymer; it does not melt and reshape.
items.random_wrong: The covalent bonds in the chains never break

items.q: Most composites are made of two materials. How are those two materials arranged?
items.correct: A matrix surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments
items.misconception: Two materials are melted into a single new substance
items.why: Both alloys and composites are 'two materials in one', so the more familiar alloy model is applied to both. In concrete you can still see the gravel in the cement. The two materials keep their own properties, which is what makes the combination useful.
items.random_wrong: Fibres surround the matrix and hold it firmly in place

items.q: Which of these materials is a composite?
items.correct: Concrete, gravel held together by cement
items.misconception: Brass, which is copper mixed with zinc
items.why: Both alloys and composites are 'two materials in one', so the more familiar alloy model is applied to both. In concrete you can still see the gravel in the cement. The two materials keep their own properties, which is what makes the combination useful.
items.random_wrong: Poly(ethene), made from many ethene units

items.q: A table gives: aluminium alloy, density 2.7 g/cm3, does not shatter; soda-lime glass, density 2.5 g/cm3, shatters when dropped; carbon fibre composite, density 1.6 g/cm3, does not shatter. Which material is lightest for a given volume and survives being dropped?
items.correct: The carbon fibre composite, the least dense
items.misconception: Aluminium alloy, since a metal can never break
items.why: One property is easier to compare than several, so the comparison stops at the first number in the table. An aircraft body made of the strongest steel would be too heavy to fly. Selecting a material means matching all the properties to the use, which is why data tables give several columns.
items.random_wrong: Soda-lime glass, since glass is the lightest here

items.q: A saucepan handle must not soften on the hot hob and must not conduct heat well. Which material is most suitable?
items.correct: A thermosetting polymer
items.misconception: A polymer with strong covalent chains
items.why: Melting is assumed to mean bond breaking, and the only bonds the student has labelled in the chain are the covalent ones. Melting separates chains from one another; it does not break the chains themselves. Only the weak forces between the tangled chains have to be overcome.
items.random_wrong: A toughened soda-lime glass

items.q: Which object is most likely to be made from bronze?
items.correct: A church bell cast in one piece
items.misconception: A trumpet played in a school band
items.why: Both alloys are copper based and both names are old and unhelpful, so the second metal is easy to swap over. Fix it by the pairing the specification gives: bronze - tin, brass - zinc. Brass instruments and door fittings are brass; statues and bells are bronze.
items.random_wrong: A knife blade that stays sharp

items.q: What is high carbon steel used for?
items.correct: Cutting tools and sharp blades
items.misconception: Car body panels and sheeting
items.why: Carbon is met as graphite in pencils, which is soft and slippery, and that image is transferred to steel. The carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and jam the layers so they cannot slide. That makes the steel hard and strong, but also brittle, so it snaps rather than bends.
items.random_wrong: Cutlery and kitchen sinks

items.q: A nail sits in a tube of dry air over a drying agent. Will it rust?
items.correct: No. Water is necessary as well as air, so dry air cannot rust iron.
items.misconception: Rusting is just iron reacting with oxygen, so air alone is enough and water only speeds it up.
items.why: Rust is iron oxide, and the word oxide points straight to oxygen, so water looks like a helper rather than a necessity. The nail over anhydrous calcium chloride has all the air it needs and still does not rust. Rusting needs both, which is why the spec says both air and water are necessary.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is corrosion another word for rusting?
items.correct: No. Rusting is one example of corrosion, the corrosion of iron.
items.misconception: Corrosion and rusting mean the same thing, so every corroding metal makes rust.
items.why: Rust is the only corrosion product most students can name, so the specific example becomes a substitute for the general term. Copper corrodes to a green coating and aluminium corrodes to a white oxide. Neither is rust. Rust is what you get when it is iron that corrodes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A painted gate is scratched. Is the iron under the scratch still protected?
items.correct: No. A barrier coating only works while it is unbroken; a scratch lets air and water reach the iron.
items.misconception: A coat of paint goes on protecting the iron even where it has been chipped or scratched through.
items.why: Barrier protection and sacrificial protection get merged into one idea called 'coating', so the property of one is credited to the other. Paint and grease work only by keeping air and water out. Break the layer and rusting starts at that spot, which is exactly why a reactive coating such as zinc is used where damage is likely.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should the oxide layer be cleaned off aluminium before use?
items.correct: No. The oxide layer is what protects the metal, so it is left in place and is often deliberately thickened.
items.misconception: The oxide layer is corrosion damage and should be removed to leave clean bright metal.
items.why: Oxide layers on iron (rust) are flaky and harmful, so the same is assumed for every metal. Rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron; aluminium oxide does not. It is a continuous layer bonded to the surface, so removing it only lets a new one form.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In galvanised iron, which metal is used up?
items.correct: The zinc is used up, because it is more reactive and corrodes in place of the iron.
items.misconception: The iron corrodes away and, in doing so, protects the zinc coating.
items.why: The word 'sacrificial' is attached to the object being protected rather than to the coating doing the protecting. The sacrifice is made BY the more reactive metal. Zinc corrodes and is slowly consumed; the iron underneath survives, which is the whole point.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are alloys softer than the pure metals they are made from?
items.correct: No. Alloys are usually harder, which is why most metals in everyday use are alloys.
items.misconception: Mixing metals dilutes them, so an alloy is always softer and weaker than a pure metal.
items.why: Mixing is associated with watering down, and the idea that pure means best carries over from everyday language. Pure metals have layers of identical atoms that slide easily. Different sized atoms in an alloy disrupt those layers, so alloys are usually harder than the pure metal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does low density mean low mass?
items.correct: No. It means low mass for a given volume; a large aluminium part can still be heavy.
items.misconception: The denser a material is, the stronger and better it is.
items.why: Density and mass are both about heaviness, and the 'per unit volume' half of the definition drops out. Density is mass divided by volume. A tonne of aluminium alloy still weighs a tonne, but it takes up far more room than a tonne of steel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a composite, which part surrounds which?
items.correct: The matrix or binder surrounds and binds together the reinforcement.
items.misconception: The fibres surround and hold the matrix in place.
items.why: The reinforcement is named as the important part, so it is assumed to be the part on the outside doing the holding. The matrix is the continuous material - the cement in concrete, the resin in fibreglass. The reinforcement is the fibres or fragments held inside it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which sodium compound goes into soda-lime glass?
items.correct: Sodium carbonate. The mixture heated is sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.
items.misconception: Sodium chloride is one of the ingredients of glass, because salt is the sodium compound you always meet.
items.why: Sodium chloride is by far the most familiar sodium compound, so it is substituted for the less familiar carbonate when the recipe is recalled. The specification names sodium carbonate. Sodium chloride is common salt and plays no part in making soda-lime glass; the third ingredient is limestone.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does 18 carat mean 18 parts of gold to 24 parts of other metal?
items.correct: No. The 24 is the whole, so 18 carat is 18 parts gold out of 24 parts of alloy, which is 75%.
items.misconception: The carat number and 24 are read as a ratio of gold to the other metals, rather than gold to the whole.
items.why: Ratios met in maths are usually part to part, like 3:2, so the fixed total of 24 is taken to be the other share instead of the total. Carats are a fraction of 24, not a ratio against 24. An 18 carat ring is 18/24 gold and 6/24 other metals, so 75% gold and 25% other metals.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.3 Using materials (chemistry only)
